newsitem.title: CONGO: Zaire's Kabila stands up Mobutu and Mandela.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Kabila stands up Mobutu and Mandela.

text.p: Rebel leader Laurent Kabila stood up Zaire's ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko but said promised peace talks at sea could go ahead on Saturday if he recieved satisfactory security guarantees.

Mobutu, who is suffering from cancer, left the converted ice-breaker SAS Outeniqua in Congo late on Friday after a day of hitches dogged efforts by South Africa's Nelson Mandela to bring the civil war rivals together, witnesses said.

Kabila's rebels, who took up arms in October and now control around three quarters of Zaire, mustered in force at Kikwit on the road to Kinshasa and pressed on regardless with their march on the capital.
"I will go to the ship tomorrow if I receive adequate assurances from the South Africans tomorrow that security arrangements are in place," Kabila told a news conference in Angola's capital Luanda.
"If we wanted to we could win this militarily in two weeks. Suggestions that I am stalling for time are ridiculous. I am interested in finding a peaceful solution to the problem."

Mobutu, his grip on Zaire crumbling after over three decades in power, is one of Africa's most enduring strongmen and was backed by the United States during the Cold War as a bulwark against Soviet communism.
He and Mandela had boarded the Russian-built Outeniqua in Pointe Noire -- Mobutu with great difficulty. Unable to climb 31 steep steps, he was driven on board five hours late up a make-shift ramp.
Kabila and Mandela's deputy, Thabo Mbeki, had been due to join the ship, a South African naval supply vessel, by helicopter in international waters off Soyo by the Angola-Zaire border.
"I am confident the two leaders realise the importance of a peaceful settlement," Mandela told reporters on the ship earlier.
There was no sign that he would leave the ship but diplomats said he was growing impatient with the delays. "We need to stop wasting time," one quoted him as saying.
Mobutu, 66, has dominated Zaire since seizing power in 1965 but prostate cancer and the whirlwind rebel offensive have weakened his grip on power in the former Belgian colony.
His aides say the talks will focus on a peaceful transition with elections open to all. They reject suggestions that the meeting is a face-saver to allow him to stand down with dignity.

Kabila, 56, says Mobutu must go and has refused to declare a truce for the talks. "There can be no ceasefire or indeed elections in this country until Mobutu and all he represents is removed and thrown away," he said on Wednesday.

A commander at rebel headquarters in the southeastern city of Lubumbashi said an airlift of rebels and equipment to the towns of Kikwit and Kananga began on Thursday and rebel forces were about to enter Kenge, 200 km (125 miles) from Kinshasa.
U.S. envoy Bill Richardson, who assisted Mandela's efforts to bring the two sides together, has said there are no conditions for the talks.
"In my view this meeting will produce a process that involves a transfer of power and hopefully a transitional inclusive government," he said on Friday.
Confusion over timing plagued the runup to the plannedc meeting, which diplomats see as a last chance to avert a potentially bloody battle for Zaire's capital of five million people.
The United States, France, Belgium and Britain have troops across the Zaire River in Congo's capital Brazzaville to evacuate their nationals from Kinshasa if need be.
